name: Prize crossword No 23,083
preamble: Most 6-letter solutions are of a kind and relate (in one case doubtfully) to 24; their solutions are undefined.

clue.text: Scrambled gold coin for English teacher

indicators.note: scrambled eggs are stirred into a mess, so the letters that follow are mixed up into a new order

blocks.note: OR is the heraldic word for gold
a ducat is an old European gold coin
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone has jumbled a gold coin to pay an English teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English teacher' reads as one phrase, but English only supplies a letter to the mix and teacher alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An educator is a general word for someone whose job is instructing pupils, a close synonym.

clue.text: Queen's number's up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: Her Majesty's time is over: the queen's number is up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number's up' is the idiom for being doomed. Per the preamble, the six-letter answer is a European capital and has no definition in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is Austria's capital.

clue.text: Overhead projector on plate between road and ship

indicators.note: something set between two things has them on either side, enclosing it

blocks.note: the M1 motorway, written MI in crosswords
the L-plate shown by a learner driver in Britain carries the letter L

explanation.surface: Instructions for setting up a classroom projector on a plate, somewhere between a road and a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overhead projector' is office equipment in the surface; read literally it is someone whose work projects over people's heads. A British L-plate marks a learner driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A hat maker produces things worn on top of the head that stick out above it, a playful cryptic description.

clue.text: Fighting talk?

blocks.note: a saw is an old saying

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fighting talk' is an idiom for aggressive words; here the two words simply give consecutive pieces. A saw is a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the Polish capital.

clue.text: Bananas free!

blocks.note: to rid is to free of something

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a market cry offering fruit at no charge. 'Bananas' is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the Spanish capital.

clue.text: Little time on boat

blocks.note: a scow is a flat-bottomed boat

explanation.surface: Someone spending a short while aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just places the second piece after the first in this down entry; mo is informal for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the Russian capital.

clue.text: It turns amphibian

indicators.note: something that turns round faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: Rana is the genus of common frogs

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests something becoming a frog. Rana is the Latin name for the frog genus.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the Albanian capital.

clue.text: Consonant consequential to vowel

blocks.note: then describes what follows as a consequence

explanation.surface: A phonetics rule about which sound follows which.
explanation.walkthrough: Literally it says a vowel, then a consonant, which spelt out is the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the Greek capital.

clue.text: Relic of summer to heartless revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolutionary overturns the existing order, so the letters are turned into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A keepsake of summer handed to a cold-hearted rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' looks like an instruction to drop middle letters, but it is part of the fodder in full.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Moore's song ''Tis the Last Rose of Summer' names the final bloom left over from the season.

clue.text: Tree preserver under fire

explanation.surface: A preserved tree that is being attacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under fire' suggests being attacked; read literally it is a container that sits below the grate collecting ashes.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashcan is a bin placed beneath a hearth or stove to catch cinders, so its position is literally below the flames.

clue.text: Is temporarily in charge of New Holidays (Thetford)

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so these letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: hols is British informal for holidays
taken as written; Thetford is a town in Norfolk

explanation.surface: A notice that someone is standing in as manager of a holiday firm called New Holidays in Thetford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Holidays' looks like a company name, but New is the anagram signal and holidays shortens to the British 'hols'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold the fort is an idiom for keeping things running while the usual person is away.

clue.text: See 10
Like Jowett with letting outside Cayenne, say?

indicators.note: to say a word is to pronounce it, so its sound is what counts, not its spelling
being outside something means surrounding it on both sides

blocks.note: the word is pronounced like the two letter names K and N

explanation.surface: A question about Jowett letting a property, apparently with cayenne pepper involved.
explanation.walkthrough: Benjamin Jowett, Master of Balliol, was mocked in verse: 'What I don't know isn't knowledge.' 'Cayenne' looks like pepper but is just two letters pronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous rhyme about the Oxford don portrays him as omniscient, claiming complete knowledge of everything.

clue.text: British (and Northeast Irish, possibly) politician would be at home in Salt Lake

definitions.text: would be at home in Salt Lake
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase rather than a noun

indicators.note: possibly signals one arrangement among several that could be made, so the letters can be reordered

explanation.surface: A British MP of Ulster-Irish roots who would feel comfortable among Utah's Mormons.
explanation.walkthrough: Salt Lake suggests Salt Lake City and its people, but the definition means the salty lake itself, where these tiny crustaceans thrive.
explanation.definitionFit: These small crustaceans live in highly saline waters, and Utah's Great Salt Lake is famous for vast numbers of them.

clue.text: Offer for Aladdin's?  The answer could be "Psalm"

blocks.note: first meaning: the wicked magician's street cry offering to swap shiny replacements for old ones, to get Aladdin's magic one
second meaning: read as an instruction, it tells you to rearrange a five-letter word into a sacred song

explanation.walkthrough: The second half works backwards: the answer itself, read as a clue, is an anagram signal followed by letters that rearrange to the given word. In the pantomime story the villain trades fresh lamps for old ones to steal the genie's lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: The magician tricks Aladdin's household by calling 'new lamps for old', so the phrase is his bargain; and the five letters rearrange to the hymn word.

clue.text: Bingham's associate in Dorset - sounds to some more like Devon!

blocks.note: surface reading: a partner of someone called Bingham who lives in the county

blocks.clueFragment: sounds to some more like Devon
blocks.note: setter's reading: the name ends in a valley word typical of Devon place names, so it sounds Devonian

explanation.surface: A Dorset man's colleague whose accent strikes some listeners as from the neighbouring county.
explanation.walkthrough: Bingham reads as a person, but Melcombe Bingham is a Dorset village name. Dorset and Devon are neighbouring English counties; combe, a small valley, ends many Devon place names.
explanation.definitionFit: The village name pairs this word with Bingham, so it is the partner of Bingham on the Dorset signpost.

clue.text: Change of sides during pestilence

indicators.note: switching sides means swapping left for right, so one letter is exchanged for its opposite

explanation.surface: Someone defecting to the enemy in the middle of an epidemic.
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for left and R for right, so changing sides swaps one for the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the Czech capital.

clue.text: Line like Rostov or Rotherham

blocks.note: both cities stand on a River Don, Rostov-on-Don in Russia and Rotherham in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A railway line that resembles two industrial river towns.
explanation.walkthrough: Rostov's full name is Rostov-on-Don; Rotherham, in Yorkshire, sits on a different River Don.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the British capital.

clue.text: Fear about wriggly worm left in Shadowlands?

indicators.note: something wriggly twists about, so its letters squirm into another order
about means around, so one piece goes round the other

explanation.surface: Someone's horror at a worm left behind in a gloomy place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shadowlands' is also the film about C.S. Lewis; the question mark marks it as a loose example of an unreal world of shadows.
explanation.definitionFit: A land of shadows is an insubstantial, illusory realm, the kind of fantasy place one escapes into.

clue.text: Make the ship secure, d'ye hear?

indicators.note: asking whether you hear points to what the words sound like when spoken

blocks.note: ships are referred to as 'her', and anchoring holds one in place

explanation.surface: A captain barking an order to make the vessel fast.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the doubtful case in the preamble: Turkey lies mostly in Asia, so its capital's link to the theme is uncertain.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this Turkish capital fits only doubtfully.

clue.text: Turn lacking vision, putting the last first

indicators.note: moving the final item to the front shifts the whole sequence round by one place

explanation.surface: A driver making a turn without being able to see, then swapping the order of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The shift moves the final letter of the joined pieces to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is the Irish capital.

clue.text: Backwater that comes back to where it started

definitions.text: that comes back to where it started

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way it came, so the letters run in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: A quiet stretch of river that curves round on itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition does double duty, also supplying the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A closed curve or circuit returns to its starting point, which is what makes it a ring or circuit.

clue.text: Ismaili leaders ask Ghana for change

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters are altered into another order

explanation.surface: Religious leaders appeal to an African nation to reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For change' sounds like asking for coins or reform, but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is held by the hereditary imams of the Nizari Ismaili Muslim community, plural here for successive holders.

clue.text: Philoprogenitive boy, loveless and cross inside

indicators.note: love is the zero score in tennis, a round letter, so being without it removes that letter
being inside means enclosed by another piece

blocks.note: the word for a lad, minus its O
a rood is a crucifix, as in rood screen

explanation.surface: A lad keen to have children, though without love and in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Cross looks like 'angry', but it is the noun for the Christian symbol. Love means nil, the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Philoprogenitive means fond of producing offspring; a broody person longs to have a baby, like a hen sitting on eggs.

clue.text: Greek well opening: what secures the bucket?

blocks.note: eu is the Greek for well, as in euphoria and eulogy
the bucket in a well hangs on a line

explanation.surface: Opening a Greek well, someone asks what holds the bucket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like a water well, matching the bucket, but it is the Greek adverb meaning good, used as the opening of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names this entry as the theme: the six-letter cities are capitals belonging to this continent.

clue.text: If this is the case, why join most of the foregoing?

blocks.note: surface reading: a debating aside, granting a premise

blocks.clueFragment: why join most of the foregoing
blocks.note: setter's reading: most of the capitals already entered belong to one European union of states, and this entry's country joined them

explanation.walkthrough: The setter's exact intent is not certain; the clue builds no letters and leans on the preamble. Most earlier capitals are in the European Union, which Portugal joined.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble says these six-letter entries are capital cities of Europe; this is Portugal's capital.
